foundations.goal: Use a route planner to distinguish acting rationally from imitating a person.
foundations.explain: Explain to a friend why asking whether a planner “thinks like a human” is different from asking whether it picks a good route.
foundations.model: A rational route planner chooses a feasible action that scores well on its stated objective using the information it has. It can do so with a hand-written travel model or a learned estimator. Human-like conversation measures a different capability.

scenes.title: Start with a goal
scenes.content: Start with one objective: reach the lecture theatre in as little time as possible. A rational planner compares its options against that objective using the information it has. Different constraints may change which routes it can choose.

check.prompt: If travel time is the only objective, which route wins?
check.hint: Choose the smallest number in the travel-time column.
check.feedback: Route A, the stairway, has the shortest predicted time at 8 minutes.

scenes.setup: A student wants to get from the library to the lecture theatre. The planner predicts the total travel times below.

scenes.title: Separate a rule from a learned estimate
scenes.content: The accessibility rule removes any route that uses stairs. The travel model estimates the total time from past trips. Once you have applied the rule, compare the estimates for the routes that remain.

check.prompt: Which step-free route has the shortest predicted travel time?
check.hint: Remove routes that violate the constraint before comparing times.
check.feedback: Route B is step-free and takes 11 minutes. Route C is also step-free but takes 14 minutes. Route A takes 8 minutes and requires stairs.

scenes.setup: The student is travelling from the library to the lecture theatre and needs a step-free route.

scenes.title: Choose a test that matches the claim
scenes.content: Thinking and acting are distinct. Acting humanly means reproducing observable human behavior. A conversational imitation test does not establish that a system plans optimal routes or performs sound reasoning.

rows: Low trip times among feasible routes

check.prompt: Which observation best checks whether the planner acts rationally?
options: It consistently chooses good feasible routes
check.hint: Look for evidence about the actual decision and its objective.
check.feedback: Route outcomes check planning performance. Conversational style measures a different skill.

scenes.setup: The same campus planner is meant to choose fast routes that meet the traveller’s accessibility needs.

state.goal: Trace one small graph before reasoning about a large search space.
state.explain: Explain why changing the order of the frontier can change the route returned even though legal moves stay the same.
state.model: The state records the robot’s room and whether it has the key. The goal is to reach the exit. OPEN determines what to inspect next. A BFS queue selects the oldest candidate and finds a fewest-edge solution with unit costs. DFS uses a stack to follow one branch at a time. A record of expanded states helps avoid repeating work and cycling in graph search.
points: Distinguish a queue from a stack

scenes.title: Model the room and the key
scenes.content: Room alone does not describe everything the robot can do. Store the room and a yes/no flag for whether the robot has the key. A visit to C before picking it up is therefore a different state from a visit to C afterward.

check.prompt: Which pair should search keep distinct?
options: States differing only in drawing position
check.hint: Ask whether both states have the same legal actions.
check.feedback: Only one state can unlock G, so merging them would lose information.

scenes.setup: The robot starts at entrance A. B is the key room, C is the corridor, and G is the exit. The exit door can be opened only if the robot has picked up the key.

scenes.title: Compare the frontier after one expansion
scenes.content: OPEN is the list of generated nodes that are waiting to be expanded. A is expanded first, putting B and C into OPEN. Next, B is taken off OPEN and generates D and E. The two strategies then arrange the remaining nodes differently.

check.prompt: Which property makes BFS choose C before D here?
options: The search has already found a goal
check.hint: A queue removes the oldest item first.
check.feedback: C was waiting before B generated D and E.

scenes.setup: This is a separate search tree. A has children B and C from left to right. B has children D and E. Start at A and use the left child first.

scenes.title: Backtrack and control depth
scenes.content: When a branch has no successors, DFS returns to a pending alternative. Depth-limited search also stops at the chosen depth. Iterative deepening raises that limit one at a time. Forward search starts with known states, while backward reasoning starts with the desired goal and works through predecessors.

check.prompt: Why might iterative deepening revisit A?
options: It starts a new depth-limited search at each limit
check.hint: Each new limit is a fresh pass.
check.feedback: Visits near the root are repeated so the algorithm can retain DFS-style space usage.

scenes.setup: Start at A. B and C are one edge away. D and E are children of B and therefore two edges from A.

heuristic.goal: Compare estimated distance with the cost you already paid.
heuristic.explain: Explain why “closest to the goal” can lead to a more expensive overall journey.
heuristic.model: Greedy best-first ranks candidates by h, the estimated remaining cost. A* adds g, the cost already paid. In our example, A has h = 1 but f = 8, while B has h = 4 but f = 6, so greedy picks A and A* picks B. With nonnegative edge costs, a consistent heuristic and the standard graph-search rules, A* returns an optimal route when it removes a goal from OPEN.

scenes.title: Distinguish local moves from a frontier
scenes.content: Hill climbing considers moves available from the current state and can stop at a local optimum or plateau. Greedy best-first compares heuristic scores among all states in OPEN, so an older branch can still be revisited if the current branch disappoints.

check.prompt: Which method can directly reconsider an older candidate kept in OPEN?
check.hint: Think about the candidates each method remembers.
check.feedback: Greedy keeps a frontier. Hill climbing usually commits to a local move.

scenes.setup: A search frontier, called OPEN, holds candidate states that have been discovered but not expanded. In the diagram, A and B are alternatives reached from Start.

scenes.title: Put paid and remaining cost side by side
scenes.content: Use road cost as g and a lower-bound estimate as h. A looks closer to the goal, but its route from the start is expensive. B has a lower combined score. When a cheaper path reaches a known state, replace its old g and recompute f.

check.prompt: Which pair is selected by greedy and A*, respectively?
check.hint: Greedy compares the h column. A* compares f.
check.feedback: Greedy chooses A because h = 1. A* chooses B because f = 6.

scenes.setup: A and B are candidates in OPEN. The table gives the actual cost from Start (g) and the estimated cost still needed to reach Goal (h).

scenes.title: Calibrate the heuristic
scenes.content: Admissibility compares h with the true cheapest remaining cost. Consistency compares neighbours: h(u) must be at most c(u,v) + h(v). With nonnegative costs, a consistent heuristic and a standard graph-search implementation support optimal A* when a goal is removed from OPEN.

check.prompt: Does this edge satisfy consistency?
options: Yes, because both estimates are positive
check.hint: Compare h(U) with the sum of the other two entries.
check.feedback: 5 > 4, so this edge violates consistency. That check alone does not establish whether the heuristic is admissible.

scenes.setup: This is a separate consistency check. U and V are two neighbouring search states connected by a directed edge U → V.

games.goal: Back up values through a game tree and see where a branch can be skipped.
games.explain: Explain to a friend why the larger leaf in a branch may carry little weight when the opponent chooses the leaf.
games.model: Every score is from MAX's perspective. At MIN, back up the smallest child. At MAX, back up the largest child. If MIN already has an option worse than what MAX can guarantee elsewhere, the rest of that branch cannot improve MAX's decision.
points: Say why the skipped leaf cannot matter

scenes.title: Predict an opponent’s reply
scenes.content: MAX chooses a branch, then MIN chooses a leaf in that branch. All utilities are measured from MAX’s viewpoint. Back up the children at each node before selecting at the root.

check.prompt: Which branch should MAX pick?
options: Either, because both have two leaves
check.hint: Look at what MIN can force in each branch.
check.feedback: MIN reduces Left to 3 and Right to 2. MAX selects 3.

scenes.setup: In this two-move game, MAX chooses Left or Right. MIN then chooses a final outcome from that branch. Every leaf score is from MAX’s point of view.

scenes.title: Carry a bound into the next branch
scenes.content: Search the left branch first, so MAX can guarantee at least 3. In the right branch, MIN sees a leaf of 2. MIN now knows that branch has value at most 2, whatever the unseen leaf is.

check.prompt: Why can the leaf 9 be skipped?
check.hint: Think about who chooses the final leaf in Right.
check.feedback: MIN has a reply worth 2 or less to MAX, so the 9 cannot make Right attractive.

scenes.setup: MAX has two MIN branches: Left has leaves 3 and 5, and Right has leaves 2 and 9. Visit Left first and visit each branch’s leaves in the listed order.

scenes.title: Know when to use an estimate
scenes.content: A full tree may be too large to finish. At a depth cutoff, use an evaluation function to estimate the value of an unresolved state. Terminal utilities still describe the actual game outcomes. Better move ordering speeds pruning while preserving minimax for the tree being evaluated.

check.prompt: If the cut occurs at a nonterminal state, where does its value come from?
options: The final outcome is already known
check.hint: At a cutoff we cannot search all the way to a final result.
check.feedback: The evaluation function estimates the unresolved position. This may change the move compared with searching to the true end.

scenes.setup: Suppose you stop one level below MAX in a game tree. Some of the nodes there are finished games and others still have legal moves.

mining.goal: Discover associations in five grocery baskets and separate frequency from usefulness.
mining.explain: Explain why a rule with high confidence can be uninteresting, then describe one way to reduce the search for frequent patterns.
mining.model: Support divides the co-occurrence count by all baskets. Confidence divides it by the baskets that contain the antecedent. Lift divides confidence by how common the consequent is across all baskets. Neither confidence nor lift establishes causation. Apriori skips supersets of infrequent itemsets, while FP-growth compresses sorted transactions into shared prefixes.
points: Explain why association is not causation

scenes.title: Turn records into a mining task
scenes.content: Association mining starts by representing each basket as a set of items. Count a basket once for each itemset it contains, even if the shopper bought several copies of the same item.

check.prompt: What is the support of {A, B}?
check.hint: Support uses the total number of baskets.
check.feedback: Two of all five baskets contain both items.

scenes.setup: A and B represent two products. Five baskets contain {A,B}, {A,B}, {A}, {B}, and {B}.

scenes.title: Compute confidence and compare a baseline
scenes.content: For A → B, condition on A. The confidence is 2/3, but B occurs in 4/5 of all baskets. Lift compares 2/3 with 4/5, giving 5/6, below one. B is less common among A baskets in this tiny sample.

check.prompt: What changes when the rule is reversed to B → A?
options: Confidence, because the antecedent now occurs 4 times
The number of baskets with both items
check.hint: The numerator is still the count of baskets containing both.
check.feedback: The new confidence is 2/4. The joint support stays 2/5.

scenes.setup: Among five baskets, three contain A, four contain B, and two contain both.

scenes.title: Find frequent patterns efficiently
scenes.content: Apriori can propose AB because A and B are frequent. AB fails the threshold, so every larger itemset containing AB fails too. FP-growth orders frequent single items by support and compresses shared prefixes. The two AB baskets still share the path B → A in the FP-tree, but its count of 2 is below the mining threshold.

rows: Only frequent sets, joined to generate candidates
Counted prefixes and conditional pattern bases

check.prompt: If AB fails the threshold, can ABC pass it?
options: Yes when the rule has high confidence
No, every ABC basket also contains AB
check.hint: Adding an item can only restrict the set of matching baskets.
check.feedback: Support is anti-monotonic under adding items, so ABC has count at most 2.

scenes.setup: In five baskets, A occurs three times, B occurs four times, and AB occurs twice. A pattern is frequent if it occurs in at least three baskets.

trees.goal: Follow a split from class counts to a predicted label.
trees.explain: Explain to someone how a tree chooses a useful question and why making every training leaf pure can backfire.
trees.model: A split is useful if the child nodes are collectively purer. Weight each child’s impurity by how many training examples it receives. Prune a brittle branch or use validation to control overfitting. Recall counts found positives out of all actual positives, including missed positives.

scenes.title: Read the label mix first
scenes.content: At the root, 4 Yes and 4 No give balance and Gini impurity 0.5. Consider two candidates with the displayed class counts. A good split reduces weighted impurity across both children.

check.prompt: Which split gives a larger Gini reduction?
check.hint: A child with only one class has impurity zero.
check.feedback: Both A children are pure, so its weighted impurity is zero.

scenes.title: Weight children and stop growing
scenes.content: Each child of B has Gini 1 − (0.75² + 0.25²) = 0.375, so weighted child impurity is also 0.375. The gain from the parent’s 0.5 is 0.125. When child sizes differ, weight each child by its share of samples. Pruning and random forests provide different ways to limit the effect of brittle branches.

check.prompt: Which child matters more in weighted impurity, one with 6 cases or one with 2?
check.hint: The weighting is proportional to the sample count.
check.feedback: The 6-case child carries 6/8 of the total weight.

scenes.setup: The parent contains eight cases: four Yes and four No. For split B, the two children contain (3 Yes, 1 No) and (1 Yes, 3 No).

scenes.title: Check who was missed
scenes.content: On held-out data, the tree found 8 true positives, missed 2 positives and flagged 4 negatives. Accuracy is 24/30, precision is 8/12, and recall is 8/10. ROC compares recall with the false-positive rate across thresholds.

check.prompt: What is recall for class Yes?
check.hint: Look only at cases that truly belong to the positive class.
check.feedback: Recall is TP/(TP + FN) = 8/(8 + 2).

scenes.setup: The confusion matrix below is for 30 held-out examples. “Yes” is the positive class.

neighbors.goal: See how a local vote differs from a maximum-margin separator.
neighbors.explain: Explain why a point that is far from a boundary may never affect an SVM even though every stored point is available to k-NN.
neighbors.model: k-NN chooses nearby labelled examples under a distance metric, then votes. A linear SVM chooses a separating hyperplane with a large margin. The nearest training points constrain the hard margin. Soft margins allow violations and penalize them.

scenes.title: Vote in a neighbourhood
scenes.content: On a line, red points lie at 1 and 3, blue points at 6 and 8, and the query is at 4. Look at distance first, then label. Standardize features when their units would otherwise give one coordinate undue influence.

check.prompt: Which class wins with k = 3?
check.hint: Read the labels of the three closest points only.
check.feedback: The nearest three vote Red, Blue, Red.

scenes.title: Find the middle of the widest gap
scenes.content: The closest opposing points are at 3 and 6, so the 1D hard-margin separator is x = 4.5. These two points are support vectors. In higher dimensions the boundary is wᵀx + b = 0 and the canonical full margin width is 2/‖w‖.

check.prompt: Which edit by itself leaves the hard-margin separator unchanged?
check.hint: Change a point that does not constrain the current margin.
check.feedback: Moving the far red point left leaves the closest opposing points at 3 and 6.

scenes.setup: On a number line, Red examples are at x = 1 and 3, and Blue examples are at x = 6 and 8. Assume a linear hard-margin SVM.

scenes.title: Allow a violation at a cost
scenes.content: If the classes overlap, a hard-margin classifier may be infeasible. A soft-margin SVM trades off a wider margin against slack penalties. Larger C gives violations more weight relative to the regularization term. Nonlinear kernels can change the geometry in which the linear separator is fitted.

rows: Greater pressure to avoid margin violations

check.prompt: If a single outlier is distorting the boundary, which change makes violations cheaper?
check.hint: C multiplies the slack penalty.
check.feedback: A smaller C can make it worthwhile to tolerate the outlier. Assess the choice on validation data.

scenes.setup: C is the parameter multiplying the penalty for margin violations in a soft-margin SVM. Keep the data and all other settings fixed.

bayes.goal: Use a population of 100 to see Bayes’ rule before using symbols.
bayes.explain: Explain why knowing that most faulty items trigger an alert does not tell you that most alerts come from faulty items.
bayes.model: Bayes reverses a conditional by combining evidence with a prior and normalizing. A rare fault starts with few items, so false alarms from the larger good group can dominate alerts. Naïve Bayes multiplies feature likelihoods within each class under conditional independence.

scenes.title: Start from the prior
scenes.content: Out of 100 items, 10 are faulty and 90 are good. A sensor alerts for 80% of faults and 10% of good items. The prior probability of a fault is the prevalence before looking at the alert.

check.prompt: How many good items generate alerts in this example?
check.hint: Take 10% of the good group only.
check.feedback: 10% of 90 is 9 false alerts.

scenes.title: Filter on the observed evidence
scenes.content: The 8 true alerts and 9 false alerts are both compatible with an observed alert. There are 17 alerts in total. The posterior P(fault given alert) is 8/17, about 47%.

check.prompt: What denominator gives P(fault given alert)?
check.hint: Restrict the total to the observed event.
check.feedback: Conditioning on alert means every denominator case must have alerted.

scenes.setup: In 100 items, 10 are faulty and 90 are good. The alert rate is 80% for faulty items and 10% for good items.

scenes.title: Combine multiple clues
scenes.content: Within each class, assume the two clues are independent. The alert and smell likelihoods are 0.8 and 0.5 for faulty items, and 0.1 and 0.2 for good items. Multiply the prior by both likelihoods to get a score. Divide a class score by the sum of the two scores to get its posterior.

check.prompt: What assumption justified multiplying the two likelihoods inside the fault class?
options: The two features are independent given the class
An alert always implies a smell
check.hint: Consider how the feature probabilities were conditioned.
check.feedback: Naïve Bayes assumes conditional independence given each class, even if features are correlated in the full population.

scenes.setup: Faulty items have prior probability 0.10. You observe both a sensor alert and an unusual smell.

neural.goal: Follow one network from prediction to a training update.
neural.explain: Explain the difference between computing a prediction and sending a training signal back through the same connection.
neural.model: A layer combines inputs with weights and biases, then applies an activation. The loss measures prediction error. Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the output toward the inputs. Gradient descent uses those derivatives to change parameters.

scenes.title: Build a forward pass
scenes.content: Use input x = 2, weight w = 1 and bias b = −1. The hidden preactivation z = wx + b = 1. ReLU returns h = 1 for positive z and zero for negative z. Let the output multiply h by another weight v = 2.

check.prompt: What would h be if b changed to −3?
check.hint: Apply ReLU after computing the new preactivation.
check.feedback: z would be −1, so ReLU clips it to zero.

scenes.title: Trace the gradient backwards
scenes.content: The target is 1 and the prediction is 2. Use L = ½(ŷ − y)². The output derivative is ŷ − y = 1. Because ReLU is active and v = 2, the gradient with respect to w is 1×2×1×2 = 4.

check.prompt: Which factor becomes zero if z is strictly negative?
check.hint: Which step is flat for negative inputs?
check.feedback: ReLU has zero derivative for strictly negative z, so this path contributes zero gradient to w.

scenes.setup: Use x = 2, w = 1, b = −1, h = ReLU(wx + b), output ŷ = 2h, and target y = 1. The current prediction is ŷ = 2.

scenes.title: Update a weight and check the result
scenes.content: With learning rate 0.1, update w to 1 − 0.1×4 = 0.6, holding all other parameters fixed. The new prediction becomes 0.4 and the loss falls from 0.5 to 0.18. In full training, also update the other trainable parameters using their own gradients. A batch determines which examples contribute to an update.

check.prompt: If a gradient is positive, what does standard gradient descent do to that weight?
check.hint: Look at the minus sign in the update rule.
check.feedback: Subtracting a positive learning-rate-scaled gradient lowers the parameter.

scenes.setup: Start from w = 1 with gradient ∂L/∂w = 4. Use x = 2, b = −1, ŷ = 2ReLU(wx + b), and target y = 1. For this example, update only w.

cnn.goal: Slide a filter, track the output shape, and pool the result.
cnn.explain: Explain why sliding the same matrix over an image uses fewer parameters than learning separate weights at every location.
cnn.model: A convolutional layer computes local weighted sums using the same filter at each position. Padding and stride set the spatial size. The number of filters sets output depth. Pooling summarizes nearby activations and reduces spatial resolution.

scenes.title: Compute one filter response
scenes.content: Use the cross-correlation convention common in CNN layers. For the patch [1, 0] on top and [2, 3] below, use a filter with top row [1, −1] and bottom row [1, −1]. Multiply aligned cells and add the products. Here the bias is zero.

check.prompt: What is the raw filter output?
check.hint: Add the two row sums.

scenes.title: Count positions and output channels
scenes.content: For a 5×5 input with a 3×3 kernel, no padding and stride 1, each axis has valid starts 0, 1, 2. This gives a 3×3 map. Two filters give two maps. Stride 2 changes the valid starts to 0 and 2.

check.prompt: If we change only the number of filters from two to four, what changes?
check.hint: Each filter produces its own channel.
check.feedback: The depth doubles. Height and width come from the spatial parameters.

scenes.setup: The image has height and width 5. Each filter has spatial size 3×3, with dilation 1 and no padding. Stride is the same on both axes.

scenes.title: Keep the strongest local activation
scenes.content: Max pooling keeps the largest activation in each window, channel by channel. It introduces no trainable weights. Using a 2×2 window with stride 2 reduces spatial resolution, so exact within-window locations are lost.

check.prompt: What does window B produce under average pooling instead?
check.hint: Add all four cells, then divide by four.

scenes.setup: Each row of the table gives a separate 2×2 pooling window in the same channel.

generalization.goal: Diagnose a model with training and validation evidence.
generalization.explain: Explain why a model can get better at its homework while becoming worse at unseen questions, and when you would stop training.
generalization.model: Training error measures fit to seen examples. Validation error estimates generalization while you tune. A widening gap with falling training error suggests overfitting. Select training choices using validation, keep the test set for the final estimate, and verify regularization empirically.

scenes.title: Read the gap
scenes.content: Suppose training error falls from 30% to 6% while validation error falls first and then rises. Late training learns details that help training predictions but transfer poorly. If both errors are high and close, investigate underfit or incomplete optimization.

check.prompt: Which checkpoint has the lowest validation error?
check.hint: Find the minimum in the validation column.
check.feedback: Epoch 3 has 17% validation error, even though epoch 4 fits the training set better.

scenes.setup: The plot and table show error rates for the same model at four checkpoints. Lower error is better.

scenes.title: Give each split a job
scenes.content: Fit model parameters and preprocessing statistics on training data. Choose hyperparameters and stopping using validation or cross-validation. Reserve test results for the final estimate. In a time-series task, also respect chronological order.

check.prompt: Where should scaling means and variances be fitted?
check.hint: Preprocessing estimates are part of fitting.
check.feedback: Fitting them on held-out data leaks information about the evaluation set.

scenes.title: Test a repair
scenes.content: A penalty such as L2 discourages large weights. Early stopping or simpler models can reduce overfit. Compare alternatives using the same validation procedure, and observe that a penalty that is too strong may harm both training and validation fit.

check.prompt: Which is best supported by these validation results?
check.hint: Use validation to judge performance on unseen data.
check.feedback: Moderate regularization has the smallest validation error here. Strong regularization appears to underfit.

clustering.goal: Use distances to group unlabelled points and see how different objectives change the grouping.
clustering.explain: Explain how k-means updates clusters and why hierarchical clustering needs a definition of distance between groups.
clustering.model: K-means alternates assignment to the closest centroid and recomputing each centroid as a mean. Agglomerative clustering merges groups by a named linkage. Both depend on scale and distance, and k-means can converge to different results from different starts.

scenes.title: Choose a useful distance
scenes.content: On coordinates like salary and age, changing currency units can move one feature from a similar scale to thousands of times larger. Euclidean distance squares coordinate differences, so unscaled units can dominate. Use scaling when comparable feature influence is appropriate.

check.prompt: Which can change Euclidean nearest neighbours without changing the people?
check.hint: Compare how coordinate units alter the numeric differences.
check.feedback: Units can change the geometry; row order and labels do not change Euclidean distances.

scenes.title: Assign and recompute
scenes.content: Start k-means at 0 and 8 on the line of points 0, 2, 7, 9. Compare distances and assign each point to the nearest centroid. Average the assigned points. Repeat until assignments stop changing or a convergence rule is met.

check.prompt: After the update, which center owns point 2?
check.hint: Its distance to the centers is 6 or 1.
check.feedback: 2 is closer to center 1. These assignments are stable here.

scenes.setup: The data are the points 0, 2, 7, and 9 on one number line. Start with centres at 0 and 8 and assign using absolute distance.

scenes.title: Define distance between groups
scenes.content: For A = {0,2} and B = {7,9}, cross-group distances are 7, 9, 5, and 7. Single linkage uses the nearest pair, complete linkage the farthest, and average linkage the mean across all pair distances. Agglomerative clustering merges the closest groups under its chosen rule.

check.prompt: Which linkage is most susceptible to chaining via a single close pair?
check.hint: Which summary can ignore the farthest pairs?
check.feedback: A single short bridge can drive a merge under single linkage.

scenes.setup: Compare the two groups A = {0,2} and B = {7,9} using absolute distance on the number line.

pca.goal: Project onto a direction, reconstruct a point, and see what you lose.
pca.explain: Explain what information PCA keeps and why a high-variance direction might still be irrelevant to prediction.
pca.model: PCA centers the data, then chooses orthogonal directions ranked by projected variance. A projection keeps coordinates along selected directions and discards the rest. High variance describes the feature cloud and does not require a target variable.

scenes.title: Center the cloud before choosing an axis
scenes.content: Subtract the feature-wise mean so the cloud is around the origin. PCA finds the first unit direction with the greatest projected variance. Subsequent directions are orthogonal, and covariance eigenvectors give the axes.

check.prompt: If the raw data cloud is translated, what should proper centering do?
options: Remove that shift from the centered cloud
check.hint: Subtracting the new mean subtracts the same shift.
check.feedback: Translation is canceled by the mean subtraction.

scenes.title: Project and reconstruct
scenes.content: Centering has already been applied. For x = (3,1) and unit axis u = (1,0), project using xᵀu = 3. To reconstruct in centered coordinates, multiply by u again, giving (3,0). The residual is (0,1).

check.prompt: If retaining only the vertical axis for this point, what is the squared residual length?
check.hint: The horizontal component would be discarded.
check.feedback: The remaining reconstruction is (0,1). The lost component has length 3, giving squared error 9.

scenes.setup: The point x = (3,1) is already centered. Compare retaining only the horizontal axis with retaining only the vertical axis.

scenes.title: Read explained variance
scenes.content: With eigenvalues 6, 3, and 1, the total centered variance is 10. Retaining one component keeps 60%, retaining two keeps 90%. Scaling changes the covariance and can change the chosen directions. The best dimension depends on the downstream goal or acceptable reconstruction loss.

check.prompt: How many components are needed to retain at least 80% in this example?
check.hint: Add the largest eigenvalues first.
check.feedback: The first two total 9 out of 10, above the threshold.

scenes.setup: Suppose a three-feature dataset has covariance eigenvalues 6, 3, and 1. These are the variances along the three principal directions.

regression.goal: Fit a line by measuring how far predictions are from actual outputs.
regression.explain: Explain why linear regression and PCA can choose different lines for the same scatter plot.
regression.model: Regression picks a response y and minimizes squared vertical errors between the observed and predicted y at each x. PCA treats both coordinates as features and measures perpendicular reconstruction errors. An outlier with an unusually large x can strongly pull a regression line, and a distant point can also change the PCA direction.

scenes.title: Define the prediction and the residual
scenes.content: For ŷ = 1 + 2x, the prediction at x = 2 is 5. If the observed y is 6, its residual y − ŷ is +1. Ordinary least squares scores the line using the sum of squared residuals across examples.

check.prompt: What is the sum of squared residuals for this line?
check.hint: Square each residual before summing.
check.feedback: 0² + (−1)² + 1² = 2. Opposite signs do not cancel.

scenes.title: Why slope and intercept work together
scenes.content: With an intercept in ordinary least squares, the fitted line passes through (x̄, ȳ). The slope is centered covariance divided by centered x variance, or the equivalent ratio of centered sums. The intercept sets the height of the line so its prediction at x̄ equals ȳ.

check.prompt: If we keep these means and the slope becomes 2, what intercept goes through the means?
check.hint: Set 5 = b + 2×2 and solve for b.
check.feedback: The intercept is 1.

scenes.setup: You want a line ŷ = b + mx through the sample means x̄ = 2 and ȳ = 5. First try slope m = 1.5, then try m = 2.

scenes.title: Distinguish the two lines
scenes.content: Ordinary regression minimizes vertical errors to predict y from x. The first principal axis of centered 2D data instead minimizes perpendicular squared distances for one-axis reconstruction. A high-leverage point can pull both lines but the objectives remain different.

check.prompt: Which method directly targets prediction of a known response column?
check.hint: Which method was told which column is the response?
check.feedback: Regression has a designated output. PCA can provide features before regression, but has a different objective.

scenes.setup: Treat the same 2D observations either as input–response pairs (x,y) or as an unlabeled point cloud. The line can solve a different task in each case.
